title: Bears From Korea's Last Bile Farm Reach New Home in Suffolk
text:
Five Asiatic black bears rescued from South Korea's bile farm are now living in a new woodland reserve in the UK, marking the first time moon bears have been relocated overseas. The journey, led by TV farmer Jimmy Doherty and supported by Space for the Wild, emphasizes the cruelty of the bile industry and the hope for future rescues.
A British wildlife campaigner has rescued five bears from tiny cages on one of South Korea's last bile farms and flown them 5,500 miles to a new home in the UK.
TV farmer Jimmy Doherty helped liberate the Asiatic black bears after they spent more than two decades confined behind rusty metal bars. The animals - Bara, Rumi, Saebit, Yong‑gi and Huimang - have now arrived at Jimmy's Farm and Wildlife Park near Ipswich, Suffolk. Confirming the news on social media on Wednesday, Jimmy said: six months ago I stood in South Korea and met these bears for the first time.
I saw the cages they had lived in and made them a promise: I would do everything I could to bring them home. Today that promise has become a reality. The rescue marks the first time moon bears have been relocated to the UK. The animals had been recovering at a specialist veterinary facility after being removed from the farm before being declared healthy enough to travel.
This is the beginning of the end of their long life in those terrible conditions on that terrible bile farm, Jimmy, patron of wildlife charity Space for the Wild, said. I can't tell you how overjoyed we are. It's been a long, long journey. The bears were transported in specially designed crates under the supervision of vets and experienced animal handlers.
A bear explores their new surroundings in Suffolk after being rescued from one of South Korea's last bile farms. A bear crosses over a bridge at the wildlife park in Suffolk, after making a safe arrival in the UK. Jimmy Doherty, patron of wildlife charity Space for the Wild, said: This is the beginning of the end of their long life in those terrible conditions on that terrible bile farm.
The bears now live in a purpose‑built woodland reserve known as Moon Bear Islands, containing trees, grass, running water and pools. The enclosure will allow the animals to forage, climb and swim after spending much of their lives standing on concrete. Moon bears are Asiatic black bears named after the distinctive pale, crescent‑shaped markings on their chests. The five bears were reportedly taken from their mothers as cubs before being confined at the bile farm.
Bara, the oldest of the group, arrived there in 1998 and remained in the same filthy metal cage for 27 years. He had reportedly never encountered a pool of water before his rescue, but began exploring a bath while recovering at the veterinary centre. Siblings Yong‑gi and Rumi spent almost two decades sharing a single barren cage, while Saebit was said to have protected the smaller Huimang during their years in captivity.
Jimmy said: Seeing them trapped in tiny cages after decades on a bear bile farm was heartbreaking. Bear farming began in South Korea in the early 1980s, when animals were imported from Malaysia and other parts of Southeast Asia. They were bred and kept for their bile and gallbladders which were used in traditional medicine and products believed to improve vitality.
The bile contains ursodeoxycholic acid, which can be used to treat some liver and gallstone conditions, although synthetic alternatives are widely available. The industry grew significantly before falling out of favour amid concerns over animal cruelty and declining demand. Around 1,000 bears were still being kept on South Korean farms in 2014. A landmark agreement was reached between the government, farmers and animal welfare organisations in 2022 to bring the trade to an end.
Breeding bears, possessing them for farming and extracting their bile were formally banned from January 1, 2026. TV farmer Jimmy helped liberate the Asiatic black bears after they spent more than two decades confined behind rusty metal bars. The animals have now arrived at Jimmy's Farm and Wildlife Park near Ipswich. Jimmy said: Six months ago I stood in South Korea and met these bears for the first time.
I saw the cages they had lived in and made them a promise: I would do everything I could to bring them home. Today that promise has become a reality. The bears were transported in specially designed crates under the supervision of vets and experienced animal handlers. The five bears relocated to Suffolk are among the first to be offered a permanent home overseas.
Jimmy warned: There's still much more to do. There are still 200 bears left here in South Korea that need help. We're working with our counterparts here in South Korea to hopefully find more homes for those other bears. Space for the Wild and Jimmy's Farm launched the Bears Behind Bars campaign to fund the animals' release, veterinary care, transport and new reserve.
The appeal has raised more than 90,000 pounds from around 3,700 donations
